analysis.one_liner: Requires airlines to pay cash compensation for delays and bumped seats, cap fees, and guarantee seat space.
analysis.headline: Introduced with four Democratic cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing or a vote in the Senate Commerce Committee and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have written a set of guarantees for airline passengers into law: at least $1,350 in cash if you are bumped from an oversold flight, automatic refunds and cash compensation when an airline's own problems delay or cancel your trip, limits on bag, change, and seat-selection fees that exceed the airline's actual costs, and a freeze on shrinking seats and legroom. It would also have let passengers sue airlines directly, banned airlines from forcing travelers into arbitration or giving up class-action rights, and raised penalties for carriers that violate passenger rules. It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Airline passengers, especially the millions who each year get bumped from oversold flights, stuck through delays and cancellations, or charged bag, change, and seat fees. Travelers with disabilities would gain enforceable rights, and anyone buying an airline ticket or joining a frequent flyer program would keep access to the courts instead of forced arbitration.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Airline passengers and flyers with disabilities

how_it_helps.text: Sets a $1,350 minimum cash payment for any passenger involuntarily denied boarding on an oversold flight, and lets airlines pay unlimited — but cash-only — incentives to volunteers, ending the current practice of offering vouchers.

Requires automatic ticket refunds when a flight is delayed or cancelled for reasons within the airline's control, plus $1,350 in cash, a meal, and hotel lodging for delays over four hours or overnight — costs the airline, not the traveler, would absorb.

Directs the Department of Transportation to bar fees for checked bags, itinerary changes, and seat selection that are 'unreasonable or disproportional' to the airline's actual cost of providing the service, and requires full disclosure of taxes and fees in any advertised or quoted price.

Orders the FAA to immediately prohibit any further shrinkage of seats, legroom, or aisle width while it writes minimum seat-size standards, and requires airlines to publish how much space each seat offers.

Gives passengers a private right to sue over unfair and deceptive practices and discrimination, voids pre-dispute arbitration clauses and class-action waivers in ticket, reward-program, and airline credit contracts, and blocks preemption of state consumer-protection claims.

Raises civil penalties on carriers that violate passenger-protection laws, prohibits airlines from negotiating those penalties down, and requires the Transportation Department to report annually on complaints it declines to act on.

analysis.who_pays: The airlines — and ultimately their customers through fares. Carriers would bear mandated compensation (up to $1,350 per affected passenger for a controllable delay or bump), automatic refunds, fee limits on what is now a multibillion-dollar ancillary-fee business, litigation exposure from a new private right of action, and higher civil penalties with no negotiated reductions. Some of that cost would predictably be passed into ticket prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Airlines, and flyers through higher fares

drawbacks.text: The costs would not stay with the airlines: mandatory cash compensation for any controllable delay over an hour, guaranteed hotel and meal coverage, and capped fees would give carriers a direct reason to raise fares or pad schedules, so frequent flyers would partly pay for the protections in the price of tickets.

The delay trigger is broad — an arrival just over one hour late for any reason 'within the control' of the carrier, including routine maintenance or IT systems, would force a full automatic refund — which is more generous than the delay rules most other countries use and would be costly for carriers during disruption-prone operations.

Creating a private right of action, allowing suits in a passenger's home state, eliminating arbitration, and expressly preserving state consumer claims would generate substantial litigation against airlines, some of it defensive, and the bill sets no cap on class-action exposure.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protections — cash compensation for bumping, refunds when an airline's own failures strand a passenger, honest all-in pricing, and a stop to ever-shrinking seats — address real, recurring harms that travelers currently absorb with vouchers or nothing, and the enforcement teeth (private lawsuits, no arbitration, higher penalties) are what make the guarantees real rather than advisory. The honest cost is that the mandates are expensive and broadly drawn, and much of the bill's price would resurface in fares; the one-hour refund trigger in particular is aggressive. On balance, the bill was designed to shift bargaining power decisively from carriers to passengers, and its costs fall mainly on a concentrated industry rather than on the public's safety or access to flying.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Blumenthal introduced the Airline Passengers' Bill of Rights on July 30, 2019, joined by four Democratic cosponsors: Senators Markey, Whitehouse, Wyden, and Casey.

The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation — the standard first step that hands a bill to the committee with jurisdiction over aviation.
No further action was ever taken: the committee held no markup or vote on the bill, it was never reported to the Senate floor, and the full action history ends with the referral.
When the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, all unfinished bills died, and the bill would have to be reintroduced from scratch in the next Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: U.S. airlines came out ahead. They kept their ancillary-fee revenue, voucher-based bump compensation, and forced-arbitration clauses, and avoided the $1,350 delay-and-bumping payments, fee limits, seat-size rules, and private lawsuits the bill would have imposed. No airline passenger gained any new protection.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: Sens. Markey, Whitehouse, Wyden, and Casey
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction — its only cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Roger Wicker (R-MS)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: U.S. passenger airlines and their trade association
against.what_they_did: The industry has a long record of opposing mandatory cash compensation for delays and bumping and limits on ancillary fees, which this bill would have imposed.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and all four cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced far enough for a vote that would have shown how the parties lined up.

industries.note: Airlines would have lost the practices the bill targets: capped voucher payouts to bumped passengers, no compensation for delays they cause, unbounded bag/change/seat fees, shrinking seats, and forced arbitration. The bill would convert what is now industry-controlled discretion into enforceable passenger rights, with cash penalties and lawsuits as the backstop.

industries.industry: Airline ancillary-fee and co-brand credit businesses
industries.note: The bill would cap fees that must be 'proportional to costs' — a direct hit to the bag, change, and seat-selection fees that have become a core airline profit center — and would void arbitration and class-action waivers in airline reward and credit-product contracts, exposing those programs to class litigation.

industries.industry: Online travel agents and flight-search platforms
industries.note: Airlines would be barred from withholding fare, fee, and schedule data and required to let these platforms sell tickets with all fees and taxes disclosed, ending the practice of steering bookings back to airline-owned channels.
